column2: the direction a working life takes over time, pictured as a curve that rises, flattens or falls

column5: a steep / flat trajectory · change / alter your trajectory
column6: Business and journalistic; everyday alternative: career path

column2: to advance step by step through the ranks of a large organisation
column3: He spent a decade climbing the corporate ladder before wondering who was holding it.
column4: She has no interest in climbing the ladder — she wants the work itself.
column5: rise through the ranks · work your way up

column2: to build a small, secure position that suits your particular strengths
column3: She carved out a niche translating patents for biotech firms.
column4: It took him years to carve out a niche in such a crowded market.
column5: carve out a role / a reputation / a career

column2: a job or experience valued mainly as a stage on the way to something better
column3: He saw the analyst role as a stepping stone to fund management.
column4: Treat the internship as a stepping stone, not a destination.
column5: a stepping stone to / towards sth

column2: a change to a different job at the same level, rather than a promotion

column5: make a sideways move · a lateral move
column6: HR-neutral; contrast: a step up · a demotion

column2: a job that offers no prospect of promotion or development

column5: be stuck in / trapped in a dead-end job

column2: to pause and assess a situation carefully before deciding what to do next
column3: Every January she takes stock of which skills still earn their keep.
column4: After the layoffs, he took stock and decided to go freelance.
column5: take stock of your career / options / finances

column2: to change professional direction strategically while keeping what already works

column5: pivot from X to Y · pivot into a field
column6: Business / startup register; neutral: change direction

column2: a planned period away from work, often for family, travel or retraining

column2: beginning to be successful and likely to become well known

column5: an up-and-coming designer / firm / district

column2: the invisible barrier that keeps certain groups, especially women, out of top positions
column3: She shattered the glass ceiling to become the bank's first female CEO.

column5: break / shatter / hit the glass ceiling

column2: to lose your job because the position itself is no longer needed
column3: Half the department was made redundant after the merger.
column4: Being made redundant at fifty pushed him into consultancy.
column5: make a post redundant · voluntary redundancy

column2: the time you must go on working between resigning and actually leaving
column3: Her three-month notice period kept her off the market until June.
column4: He negotiated a shorter notice period before signing the contract.
column5: work out / serve your notice period

column2: to formally tell your employer you are leaving
column3: She handed in her notice the day her visa cleared.
column4: He had been threatening to hand it in for a year before he finally did.
column5: give in / work your notice · notice period

column2: to leave a senior position voluntarily, especially so that someone can replace you
column3: The chairman stepped down after twelve years at the helm.
column4: She stepped down as head of research to return to the lab.
column5: step down as chair · step down from a post

column2: to do someone's job temporarily while they are away

column6: Neutral; formal: deputise for sb · also: cover for sb

column2: to approach someone who already has a job and persuade them to join another company

column2: the trial months in a new job during which either side can end the contract easily

column4: His contract was not renewed at the end of the probationary period.
column5: complete / pass / extend a probationary period

column2: to dismiss workers because there is not enough work, usually in large numbers

column4: Tech firms have been laying off staff all year.
column5: mass layoffs · be laid off

column4: Read the severance terms before you resign, not after.
column5: a severance package / agreement

column2: to select the few strongest candidates for final consideration
column3: Two hundred people applied; nine were shortlisted.
column4: Her portfolio got her shortlisted for the design prize.
column5: be shortlisted for a post · draw up a shortlist

column2: the rate at which employees leave an organisation and are replaced

column4: Turnover fell sharply once flexible hours came in.
column5: high / low / rapid staff turnover

column2: to have more experience or education than a job requires — and so be unlikely to stay
column3: They rejected her as overqualified for the coordinator role.

column5: be overqualified for a post

column2: a job that is available for someone to take

column5: fill / advertise a vacancy

column2: to lure an employee away from another company, often a direct rival
column3: Their entire data team was poached by a hedge fund.
column4: We lost two engineers to poaching last quarter.
column5: poach staff / talent / clients from a rival

column2: to accept an amount of work, especially a large one
column3: She took on a workload designed for two people.
column4: Don't take on more than the role actually pays for.
column5: take on work / staff / responsibility · a heavy workload

column2: to finish a piece of work by the agreed time
column3: We met the deadline with forty minutes to spare.

column5: meet / miss / extend / set a deadline · a tight deadline

column2: to have far more work than you can deal with
column3: I'm completely snowed under this week — can it wait until Monday?
column4: The support team has been snowed under since the update shipped.
column5: snowed under with work / emails / requests

column2: to finally start working seriously and with full attention
column3: It's time to knuckle down and finish the application.

column5: knuckle down to work / to revision
column6: Informal; neutral: apply yourself, get down to work

column2: (of work) requiring great effort but giving deep satisfaction — the classic job-ad pairing
column3: Teaching is demanding yet rewarding in roughly equal measure.

column5: a demanding role / schedule · deeply rewarding

column2: to work continuously, day and night
column3: The legal team worked around the clock to close the deal.
column4: You cannot run a company by working around the clock yourself.
column5: work around the clock to do sth · round-the-clock support

column2: to do your fair share of the shared work
column3: Everyone here pulls their weight — there is nowhere to hide.
column4: He was let go for simply not pulling his weight.
column5: pull your weight in a team

column2: to give parts of your work, and the authority for them, to other people
column3: Learn to delegate, or your team will never grow.
column4: She delegates the routine and keeps the judgement calls.
column5: delegate tasks / authority / responsibility to sb

column2: to try to manage several conflicting duties at the same time
column3: Working parents juggle competing demands every single day.
column4: He was juggling three clients' demands from two screens.
column5: juggle work and family · juggle priorities

column2: to spend a great deal of time working
column3: She put in brutal hours all through the audit season.
column4: Partners are expected to put in whatever hours the deal requires.
column5: put in long hours / a full shift / overtime

column2: to stay in control of work that keeps arriving, so that it never piles up
column3: A daily fifteen-minute sweep keeps me on top of my inbox.
column4: Once you stop keeping on top of the paperwork, it buries you.
column5: keep on top of your workload / admin / emails

column2: a deadline that is approaching fast and beginning to cause worry
column3: The looming deadline concentrated everyone's minds wonderfully.
column4: With the deadline looming, they quietly cut half the features.
column5: a deadline looms · with sth looming

column2: physical and emotional collapse caused by prolonged overwork

column4: She recognised the burnout only after her doctor named it.
column5: suffer / experience burnout · be heading for burnout

column1: burn the candle at both ends
column2: to exhaust yourself by working late and getting up early, day after day

column4: Burn the candle at both ends in your twenties and the invoice arrives in your thirties.
column5: (fixed idiom — used whole)

column2: to work until your health or judgement gives way
column3: She ran herself into the ground getting the launch out on time.
column4: Don't run yourself into the ground for a company that would replace you within a week.
column5: run sb / yourself into the ground

column2: the healthy division of time and energy between work and the rest of life

column4: The four-day pilot measurably improved staff's work-life balance.
column5: strike / maintain / improve a work-life balance

column2: to cause gradual, cumulative damage
column3: The commute was quietly taking its toll on her health.
column4: Years of shift work take their toll eventually.
column5: take its toll on health / morale / relationships

column2: to have your time and energy divided among so many duties that none is done well
column3: With two vacancies unfilled, the team is stretched dangerously thin.
column4: She was stretched so thin that even small requests felt heavy.
column5: be stretched thin / to the limit

column2: to stop thinking about work and let your mind rest
column3: Remote workers find it far harder to switch off at the end of the day.
column4: He cannot switch off unless the phone stays in another room.
column5: switch off from work · fully switch off
